Reading

Part 1: One Word, Many Dishes

When people in Japan hear "curry," they may picture a thick brown sauce with rice, potatoes, carrots, onions, and meat.

However, curry is not one recipe.

Across South Asia and other parts of the world, cooks make many different dishes with spices.

Some are dry, some have a lot of sauce, and some use coconut milk or tomatoes.

Many of these dishes also have their own local names.

The wide English word "curry" became common through British colonial contact with South Asia.

It is useful as a big food category, but it cannot show every local tradition.

Reading

Part 2: Meet the Spice Team

There is no single spice mix for every curry.

One curry powder may contain turmeric, coriander, cumin, chili pepper, fenugreek, cinnamon, cardamom, black pepper, and more.

Think of the spices as a team.

Turmeric often brings yellow color and an earthy note.

Cumin gives a warm, rich smell.

Coriander seed can add a lighter, slightly citrus-like taste.

Chili pepper brings the burning feeling we call heat.

Cinnamon and cardamom can add a sweet aroma.

A cook changes the amount of each spice to build a different result.

That is why two curries can smell and taste very different.

Reading

Part 3: Heat, Aroma, and Depth

Here is a useful curry test: notice heat, aroma, and depth.

Heat is the burning feeling from chili.

Researchers explain that capsaicin, a substance in chili peppers, activates nerves that also respond to heat.

Your curry can therefore feel hot even when its temperature is not very high.

Aroma is what reaches your nose, such as warm cumin or sweet cardamom.

Depth means the flavor feels full rather than simple.

Onions, garlic, ginger, toasted spices, broth, fat, and cooking time can all add depth.

A curry can be mild but still have a strong aroma and deep flavor.

Reading

Part 4: Curry Gets a Passport

Japanese curry has a travel story with several stops.

Its deeper roots are in South Asian spice traditions.

Under British colonial rule, British cooks and companies turned the idea into commercial curry powder.

The powder made a complex mix of spices easier to buy and move.

This British-style product then entered Japan in the Meiji period, when many Western foods were becoming known there.

Japanese cooks did not simply copy one Indian dish.

They received a British version and changed it again for local ingredients, rice, and everyday meals.

Imagine a curry passport with three stamps: South Asia, Britain, and Japan.

Reading

Part 5: Japan Makes Curry Its Own

In Japan, curry became a thick sauce served over rice.

Carrots, potatoes, onions, and meat became common ingredients.

One well-known story connects this style with the Japanese Navy.

Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries presents it as one theory, not the only story.

British naval curry was thickened, paired with rice, and used as a practical meal with meat and vegetables.

Retired sailors later helped spread naval-style curry in Japan.

Whether people met curry through the navy, restaurants, or home cooking, the important point is adaptation: the dish changed to fit Japanese rice and daily life.

Reading

Part 6: The Curry Shortcut

Curry became easier to cook when ready-made products improved.

In 1923, food maker Minejiro Yamazaki produced the first curry powder made in Japan.

In 1930, his company began selling the first curry powder for household use in Japan.

Curry roux later made the process even simpler.

Roux blocks contain flour, oil or fat, spices, seasonings, and other ingredients.

A home cook can prepare meat and vegetables, add water, and melt the roux into the pot.

The sauce becomes thick and gets a steady flavor.

Curry roux is like a shortcut: it turns a large spice team into one easy block.

Reading

Part 7: Foreign, Familiar, and Fun

Japanese curry often feels different because several choices work together.

The sauce is usually thick, it is served with short-grain rice, and cooks can choose mild, medium, or hot roux.

Onions or fruit may add sweetness in some recipes.

Many people meet curry at home, in restaurants, or at school lunch, so its smell can bring back personal memories.

Curry began with ideas from outside Japan, but Japanese cooks and diners made it familiar.

That is cultural adaptation: a food travels, changes, and becomes part of a new place.

Curry is foreign and Japanese at the same time—and that is what makes its story fun.
